item.title: Dynamic Preference Logic of Preference Lifting
item.description: arXiv:2611.26643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In preference logic, preference is modeled as a binary relation between possible worlds. When we discuss preference relations between propositions, we also need to consider how to lift this relation between possible worlds to propositions. Here, propositions are usually represented by their extensions, that is, sets of possible worlds. There are several choices of lifting scheme: for example, one may require even the worst world in one set to be better than the best world in another, or merely require that every world in one set have some better world in the other. The framing effect in behavioral economics shows that the lifting scheme can change with the way a question is posed or with psychological factors. This paper proves that such changes cannot be reduced to changes in preferences between possible worlds. Accordingly, we treat the lifting scheme as an independent dimension of evaluation and use a hybrid language to describe switches between lifting schemes. We thereby present a language for preference logic with dynamic lifting and prove its soundness and completeness.
item.dc:creator: Xiaochen Chang

item.title: Littlestone Dimension and Its Dual
item.description: arXiv:2611.26721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dual Littlestone dimension of a concept class $\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$, $\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}):=\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H}^*)$, is the Littlestone dimension of the dual class $\mathcal{H}^*$, obtained by exchanging the roles of domain points and hypotheses. A classical result of Shelah implies that $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})$ and $\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H})$ are finite simultaneously, and quantitative results of Hodges [Mathematika, 1981] imply the doubly exponential bound $\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le 2^{2^{O(\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H}))}}$. Malliaris and Moran [Trans. Amer. Math. Soc., 2024] asked whether this bound is optimal. We answer this by proving the improved bound \[ \operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal{H})\le 2^{O(\operatorname{Ldim}^*(\mathcal{H})^2)}. \] An exponential dependence is necessary, as witnessed by the class of all binary hypotheses on a finite domain.
item.dc:creator: Pooya Hatami, Chavdar Lalov

item.title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments
item.description: arXiv:2611.26869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Berkholz, Hubie Chen

item.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
item.description: arXiv:2611.26906v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.
item.dc:creator: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang

item.title: Moonshine Conjecture Formalized
item.description: arXiv:2611.27001v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The celebrated and intimidating Moonshine Conjecture has now been formalized in Lean. This achievement might suggest that, once a sufficiently large library compiles, the principal mathematical work is complete. This paper tells a less optimistic story. During our formalization project, we repeatedly encountered two problems that a formally checked proof alone does not settle: (1) whether the formal statements actually express the mathematics we humans expect, and (2) how that meaning survives as the repositories and their dependencies evolve. We argue that there is no magic pill that turns a large agent-produced library into mathematics a community can trust. Even after the proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, someone must judge whether the definitions and statements express the intended mathematics and whether future updates preserve that meaning. This work, even when done, can only be trusted. We must therefore return to the usual trust model: relying on the mathematical judgment of maintainers and expert communities. But semantic review is expensive, making it tempting to keep producing code and take successful kernel checks as sufficient grounds for trust. This shortcut accumulates semantic debt: definitions and results with unchecked mathematical interpretations are reused as foundations for further work. A library may keep compiling and produce the desired formal theorem while users lose track of which mathematical claims they can responsibly rely on. Reliable reuse is also a prerequisite for Terence Tao's vision of formal mathematics as something people can navigate, explain, learn from, and build with. This paper takes our work connecting the VOA and CFSG repositories for the Moonshine Conjecture as a case study of the challenges of reliable reuse as formal developments scale.
item.dc:creator: Jin-Cheng Guu

item.title: No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.27260v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent. We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error. Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Amer, Loren Kinczel, Darrell D. E. Long

item.title: Bounded Treewidth Rulesets Are Not Finitely Controllable
item.description: arXiv:2611.27461v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An ontology language $O$ is finitely controllable with respect to a query language $Q$ if the finite and unrestricted variants of the query entailment problem for $\langle O, Q\rangle$ coincide. In this paper, we study finite controllability (FC) in its classical sense for existential rules, where $O$ is a class of existential rules and $Q$ is the class of all Boolean conjunctive queries (BCQs). A natural question in this line of work is whether the class of bounded treewidth sets (BTS) is finitely controllable with respect to BCQs. We answer this question negatively: we exhibit a simple set of rules over a binary signature and prove that it is BTS but not FC. Moreover, using the same set of rules, we show that two subclasses of BTS, namely GBTS and pieceful, are not FC either.
item.dc:creator: Piotr Ostropolski-Nalewaja, Micha\"el Thomazo

item.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
item.description: arXiv:2611.27489v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.
item.dc:creator: Oliver Sch\"on, Adrien Banse, John Lygeros, Lars Lindemann

item.title: Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^{3/2}$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.27814v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $\epsilon >0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{\frac{3}{2}-\epsilon})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $\epsilon > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{\frac{3k}{2}-\epsilon})$, where $N$ is the input size. Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.
item.dc:creator: A. R. Balasubramanian, Rupak Majumdar

item.title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.27865v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.
item.dc:creator: Arshia Rafieioskouie, Matthew Lucas, Tzu-Han Hsu, Borzoo Bonakdarpour

item.title: QANAD: A Model-Driven Framework for Quantitative Analysis and Synthesis of Activity Diagrams via Probabilistic Model Checking
item.description: arXiv:2403.00169v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probabilistic model checking is a widely used formal verification technique to automatically verify qualitative and quantitative QoS properties for probabilistic models, such as reliability, performance, and cost. However, devising suitable and representative models for systems of interest in model checkers, writing corresponding properties, and verifying them requires domain knowledge in probabilistic models, formal verification, and the target model checkers. This unavoidably makes model checking not easily accessible for researchers and engineers who may lack the required knowledge. Previous work has extended UML activity diagrams with probability and time, along with quality annotations, developed transformations from activity diagrams to probabilistic models which model checkers support, and implemented accompanying tools for automation. The research, however, is fragmented, informal, or not fully open, making its use, extension, and adaptation non-trivial. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce QANAD, a comprehensive verification framework for activity diagrams, that includes a new profile for probability, time, parameters, and quality annotations, a semantics interpretation of activity diagrams in Markov models variants (DTMCs, MDPs, and CTMCs) and their parametric versions, and a set of formal transformation rules from activity diagrams to the PRISM modelling language, supported by the leading model checkers PRISM and Storm. The theory underpinning QANAD has been realised into transformation implementation using model-driven engineering, enabling fully automated model transformation with automated verification using (parametric) probabilistic model checking and semi-automated synthesis. We demonstrate QANAD on a case study where multiple robots are used for delivery in a hospital environment and evaluated six other examples from the literature.
item.dc:creator: Kangfeng Ye, Fang Yan, Simos Gerasimou

item.title: Characterization and Decidability of FC-Definable Regular Languages
item.description: arXiv:2505.09772v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: FC is a first-order logic that reasons over all factors of a finite word using concatenation, and can define non-regular languages like that of all squares (ww). In this paper, we establish that there are regular languages that are not FC-definable. Moreover, we give a decidable characterization of the FC-definable regular languages in terms of algebra, automata, and regular expressions. The latter of which is natural and concise: Star-free generalized regular expressions extended with the Kleene star of terminal words.
item.dc:creator: Sam M. Thompson, Nicole Schweikardt, Dominik D. Freydenberger

item.title: When are two algorithms the same? Towards addressing Hilbert's 24th problem
item.description: arXiv:2508.02764v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The informal question of when two theorem proofs are "essentially the same" goes back to David Hilbert, who considered adding it (or something largely equivalent) to his famous list of open problems, but eventually decided to leave it out. Given that the notion of a formal proof is closely related to that of a (computer) program, i.e. a recursive function, it may be useful to ask the same question with regard to programs instead. Here we propose a minimalistic approach to this question within Recursion Theory, building heavily on the use of Kolmogorov Complexity.
item.dc:creator: Konstantin Doubrovinski
